newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: AUSTRALIA EXPRESSES REGRET AT SOUTH PACIFIC DOCUMENT LEAK
Australia has expressed regret at the leaking of a secret briefing document on the South Pacific.
The Foreign Minister, Alexander Downer made the comment in Fiji after talks with Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka.
Mr Downer said Australia and Fiji were important partners in the region with strong links and common interests.
He said the recent regrettable incident involving the publication of controversial material would not change the importance, nor he trusted the closeness of that partnership.

"Indeed it was unfortunate that the media attention in Australia over briefing material side-tracked attention from what was indeed a very successful Forum Economic Ministers meeting in Cairns last July," he said.
"Let me repeat once and for all that the media reports and comments do not reflect the view or attitude of the Australian government nor Australian government policy towards island countries."
AUSTRALIA'S CAUTIOUS WELCOME OF S.PACIFIC FREE TRADE AREA
Australia has given a cautious welcome to the idea of a South Pacific free trade area.
Speaking in Suva today, Foreign Minister, Alexander Downer said a free trade in the South Pacific might be worth while, but the idea had to be examined further.

Mr Downer said to help move the process forward he had asked the Australian aid agency AUSAID to commission a study of the costs and benefits of a regional free trade agreement for individual Pacific Island countries, as well for Australia and New Zealand.
"Australia's concerned that a free trade area be to the benefit of all countries not just to the benefit of some," Mr Downer said.
"If implemented, it may be a useful mechanism it may turn out to be a very important mechanism to bind countries in the region more closely together," he said.
SURGEONS FACE UP-FRONT QUOTES TO PRIVATE PATIENTS
Surgeons will be required to provide private hospital patients with up-front quotes on the cost of medical treatment, under changes agreed to by Federal Cabinet today.
The reforms are aimed at stemming the decline in private health insurance membership.

Federal Health Minister Michael Wooldridge said the move to ensure pre-surgery quotes were provided would give patients much greater certainty and reduce the problem of large and unexpected out of pocket costs.
As well, Cabinet has decided to extend the waiting period before new health fund members get access to benefits for obstetrics from nine to 12 months.
The reform package also provides incentives for private hospitals to strike deals with doctors over surgery bills.
Dr Wooldridge said the Government was determined to do everything in its power to make private health insurance more attractive and more affordable.
FEDERAL CABINET REJECTS HEROIN TRIAL
Federal Cabinet has decided not to support the ACT's proposed heroin trial.
Cabinet has decided it will not pass the necessary legislation to allow heroin to be imported for the trial, or provide financial support.
The Prime Minister said the Cabinet decision would apply to any other state or territory which proposed such a trial.
Mr Howard said it was a difficult issue for both the Government and the community.
"Anybody who imagines that I sort of have an open and shut view on this issue is wrong," Mr Howard said.
"I agonised over it. I talked to a lot of people about it. And the view that I've taken is that on balance, I'm sure it's the right view," he said.
A long-time campaigner for the heroin trial, Michael Moore, said Cabinet's decision was a disgrace.
Mr Moore, an Independent member of the ACT Legislative Assembly, said a media campaign against the trial appeared to have worked.
"Of course I'm disappointed. But I'm even more disappointed at the Prime Minister saying it was an on-balance decision. It wasn't an on-balance decision it was made on moral rectitude.
"It was made on ignorance and it was built on fear, and it was pushed by Rupert Murdoch and one of his rags," Mr Moore said.
OPPOSITION SHOWN EFFECTS OF CLOTHING TARIFF CUTS
The textile, clothing and footwear industry's campaign against tariff cuts continues to gather momentum.
The industry held a fashion parade in Melbourne, to show what would be lost in terms of local production if import tariffs were reduced.
High ranking members of the Australian fashion industry joined Shadow Industry Minister Simon Crean and Shadow Minister for Training Martin Ferguson at the parade.

Mr Crean said the Prime Minister John Howard was forced into the automotive industry tariff freeze and he should be aware it would be just as tough to cut tariffs in the textile, clothing and footwear industry.
"Keep the pressure up. This is a Government, but in the end it crumbles to pressure," Mr Crean said.
"It did in the car industry. It did on the ship building industry.
"It did with relation to the book publishing industry. All decisions reversed because the pressure was focused on them," he said.
MAN FACES FIVE MURDER CHARGES
A fresh murder charge has been laid against a 42-year-old man, extradited from Adelaide to Sydney four months ago.
Lindsay Robert Rose appeared in Sydney's Central Local Court charged with the murder of Reynette Holford at West Ryde in 1987.
It is the fifth murder charge New South Wales police have laid against Mr Rose.
Shortly after his extradition from Adelaide in April, he appeared in court charged with the murders of two people in a Gladesville massage parlour in 1994 and a couple at Hoxton Park in 1984.
Bail has again been refused for Mr Rose, who is expected to face committal proceedings in September.
ACCOUNTANTS WANT TAX COLLECTION CLARIFIED
The business sector is applying pressure to the Howard government to come up with a clear plan on how new Federal taxes on tobacco, liquor and petrol are to be collected.

The Institute of Chartered Accountants and the New South Wales Chamber of Commerce say the government has given itself six months to sort out who is going to collect the taxes, from whom and at what rate.
But after a forum with representatives of the tobacco, petrol and liquor industries, they say the government should devise a plan much sooner.
The Institute's Martin Fiel says tobacco industry representatives have indicated they have given up on discussions about collecting the taxes and obtaining refunds, because it's too complicated.
"In six weeks we really should be able to have a comprehensive well thought out process for something that's as important as this. We shouldn't have to wait six months," Mr Fiel said.
"We really should have something that's a very transparent process so that the consumers and the companies know that they are getting as equitable a deal as possible," he said.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
